dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — and a big welcome to Benji, who arrived this weekend after Saturday night's hospital trip. It is a cloudy, mild Monday in Solon, high near 64°, with no rain expected and the first early sunset of standard time at 5:19 tonight. Overnight, Iran left the Doha talks with a draft U.S. deal circulating that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the naval blockade ends, while Senator Chris Murphy was hospitalized after a stroke at his son's hockey game, with a full recovery expected. There is no early voting today, so tomorrow is the day: polls are open 6:30 AM to 7:30 PM for the midterms, and 66 Cuyahoga County precincts — including some in Solon — have new polling places, so check yours before you go. Tonight's home entertainment is set too, with the Cavs hosting Oklahoma City at Rocket Arena at 7 PM.

Election week dominates the calendar: there is no early voting today, polls are open Tuesday 6:30 AM to 7:30 PM with 66 Cuyahoga precincts at new locations including in Solon, and Ohio's tight governor's and Senate races top the ballot. In sports, the Cavs host Oklahoma City tonight, the Browns travel to New Orleans on Sunday, and Ohio State hosts Oregon on Saturday afternoon. The standout deal remains Giant Eagle's BOGO-free sirloin tip roasts through Wednesday — and at home, this is Benji's first week: newborn days, a first pediatrician check a few days after discharge, and Moose waiting to meet the newest Smiley.

items.title: Cavs vs Oklahoma City Thunder
Iran negotiators leave Doha as a draft U.S. deal circulates
items.summary:
Iranian negotiators have left talks in Doha with Qatari mediators, and a draft proposal for a deal with the United States is now circulating, an official briefed on the talks said Monday. The team departed Sunday, reportedly not because the talks had broken down, and a follow-up meeting is possible.

Tehran says the starting point is its seven-step plan from September to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the U.S. naval blockade. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said the strait could reopen on a two-day timeline if conditions are met, a much faster version than first proposed. An earlier Iranian proposal was rejected by President Trump.

Nothing has been agreed yet. Trump has said the U.S. will not launch new attacks before Tuesday's vote and called the talks productive, without ruling out action later. The gap is still over what Washington must do first, and over Iran's broader demands.

Watch for a public U.S. response to the draft and any date for negotiators to return to Doha.

items.title: Israel deadlocked after its election as Lieberman backs Eisenkot over Netanyahu
items.summary:
Avigdor Lieberman said Monday that his Yisrael Beiteinu party will back Gadi Eisenkot of the Yashar party to form Israel's next government, ruling out sitting in a government led by Benjamin Netanyahu. He also ruled out propping up a minority government, saying it could fall within a year.

Last week's election left no bloc close to power on its own. Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, opposition parties won 48 and Arab parties won 19, and 61 seats are needed to govern. Support for Eisenkot is also growing elsewhere in the opposition, including from Naftali Bennett's bloc, and Arab lawmakers may back him to block Netanyahu.

Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister until a new government is sworn in. President Isaac Herzog begins consultations on November 4, and whoever is nominated will have 28 days, plus a possible 14-day extension, to win a confidence vote.

The new parliament convenes November 10. The next few weeks will show whether an anti-Netanyahu majority can actually agree on a government, or whether Israel heads toward another stalemate.

items.title: Spain identifies 66 of the 69 people killed in the Urda train crash, including four Americans
items.summary:
Officials in Spain have identified 66 of the 69 people killed in last Wednesday's train crash near Urda, south of Madrid, the regional high court said Monday. Three cases are still pending and are believed to involve foreign nationals whose families are traveling to Spain.

Of those identified, 54 were Spanish and 12 were foreign citizens, including four Americans and one person each from Argentina, Canada, the Czech Republic, France, Japan, Mexico, Portugal and Tunisia. Most identifications were made by fingerprints, with the rest confirmed by DNA. Sixty families have been formally notified so far.

The crash happened on October 28 when a Renfe high-speed train hit the rear of a stationary Iryo train on the Madrid-Seville line. It left 41 people in hospital, 16 of them in intensive care in the latest count.

Spain's government was expected to approve financial aid for those affected on Tuesday. Three missing-person reports remain open while the last identifications are completed.

items.title: Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian refineries as Moscow hits its power grid
items.summary:
Ukraine has resumed long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, targeting the Kstovo refinery in the Nizhny Novgorod region overnight Sunday after a strike Friday on the Novokuybyshevsk refinery in Samara. The renewed campaign comes despite U.S. pressure on Kyiv to pause attacks on energy sites.

Ukrainian officials said they never agreed to a proposed 30-day halt on refinery strikes. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy defended the attacks as a response to Russian strikes on Ukraine's energy system, which he said left hundreds of thousands of households without power across four regions overnight.

Russia said it shot down 235 Ukrainian drones overnight, while Ukraine said it downed 371 of 433 Russian long-range drones launched since Saturday evening. The Nizhny Novgorod governor said a large industrial site suffered significant damage.

The exchange shows the energy war escalating on both sides heading into winter, even as separate diplomacy over shipping and gas continues in the background.

items.title: U.N. peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara ends after 35 years
items.summary:
The United Nations mission in Western Sahara has ended operations after 35 years, with a liquidation period beginning November 1. A smaller U.N. team will now handle moving equipment and assets back to the countries that contributed them.

The mission, known as MINURSO, was set up in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire and prepare a referendum on self-determination that never happened. It ended after Russia vetoed a U.S. draft resolution on Friday and a rival Russian plan to extend the mission was voted down. The mission had 534 authorized personnel and a budget of more than $62 million.

Morocco welcomed the outcome. The Algeria-backed Polisario Front called it unacceptable, and Algeria said it deeply regrets the decision. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres remains concerned about security and has urged all sides to show maximum restraint.

Without peacekeepers on the ground, there is less independent monitoring along the berm dividing the territory, raising the risk that a long-frozen conflict could heat up again.

items.title: France opens attempted-murder probe after a petrol bomb is thrown at police in Paris
items.summary:
Paris prosecutors have opened an attempted-murder investigation after incendiary devices were thrown at security forces at the end of a Saturday demonstration at Porte de Charenton. About 15 gendarmes and police were targeted, and images showed a device exploding at an officer's feet and setting protective gear alight.

Reported injuries included second-degree burns and tinnitus, though officials said the assessment was still provisional. No one had been arrested specifically for that attack at the time of reporting. Nationwide, the Interior Ministry put arrests during the demonstrations and Halloween night at 779, including 105 in Paris, lower than the previous two weekends.

The march was part of a third weekend of protests over high living costs and government policies. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez condemned the attack in the strongest terms.

Investigators must now identify who threw the devices. Whether the next round of demonstrations stays peaceful will shape how the government responds to a protest movement that has not faded.

items.title: Final Senate polls put Democrats ahead in the battlegrounds, most of them close
items.summary:
Democrats lead in the final New York Times/Siena polls of the seven Senate battlegrounds that will likely decide control of the chamber, released on the eve of Election Day. Michigan is the widest gap, with Abdul El-Sayed at 53% to Mike Rogers at 42%, and Texas is next, with James Talarico at 50% to Ken Paxton at 43%.

The other races are tighter: Sherrod Brown leads Jon Husted 49% to 44% in Ohio, Troy Jackson leads Susan Collins 51% to 45% in Maine, and Adam Hamilton leads Roger Marshall 49% to 44% in Kansas. Alaska and Iowa are within the margin of error. The surveys covered 5,708 likely voters from October 23 to November 1.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take the Senate. President Trump's approval in these states was 38%, described in the polling coverage as historically low for a president heading into a midterm.

Polls are not results, and several of these leads sit inside or near the margin of error. Tuesday's turnout will decide whether the polling picture holds.

items.title: Trump administration asks the Supreme Court to set aside 20,000 California ballots
items.summary:
On the eve of the election, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to block California from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters federal officials say are likely noncitizens, until each voter's citizenship is verified. The Justice Department argues that once those ballots are mixed with lawful ones, they cannot be separated again.

Two courts have already said no. A federal judge denied the request on October 28, and the 9th Circuit refused it 2-1 on Friday, pointing to California's own election safeguards and the state's power over election procedures. California officials also say many people on the federal list do not have active registrations and were not sent ballots, so the real number in dispute is likely much smaller.

The list was assembled by the Department of Homeland Security and sent to California and Los Angeles County. The emergency request goes to Justice Elena Kagan, who handles applications from that circuit.

A decision could come at any time, but election-law experts note courts are usually reluctant to change voting rules this close to an election.

items.title: Stevens endorsement fallout deepens in Michigan as El-Sayed raises millions in hours
items.summary:
The fallout from Rep. Haley Stevens endorsing Republican Mike Rogers for Senate in Michigan rolled into Monday. Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to Abdul El-Sayed, explained her decision in a new interview by criticizing El-Sayed's focus on Israel, after appearing with Rogers at a Detroit church on Sunday.

Democratic leaders reacted sharply over the weekend, with Senate Leader Chuck Schumer calling it a betrayal and the Michigan Democratic Party chair saying Stevens was no longer a party member. Several of her staff resigned. President Trump praised the endorsement at a rally and urged her to join the Republican Party.

El-Sayed's campaign said it raised $2.4 million on Sunday after the endorsement, and he told reporters in Ypsilanti on Monday that he did not want to dwell on it, framing the race as a referendum on Trump through Rogers.

Michigan's open seat has not elected a Republican senator since 1994. Whether the endorsement moves late undecided voters, or mainly energizes El-Sayed's base, will only be clear on Tuesday.

items.title: Trump makes his closing midterm pitch at the Reflecting Pool after a final rally weekend
items.summary:
President Trump closed his midterm campaign Monday with a speech focused on the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, billed as his final scheduled pitch before Tuesday's vote. He did not mention the election until about 22 minutes into the remarks, according to live coverage.

The speech followed rallies Sunday in Dubuque, Iowa, and Salina, Kansas, where he campaigned for Senate candidates Ashley Hinson and Roger Marshall and told supporters a Republican House and Senate would keep his agenda moving. He has held more than two dozen rallies in 19 states since October 1.

All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot Tuesday, deciding control of Congress for Trump's final two years. Speaker Mike Johnson joined him in Iowa and urged voters to dismiss polling showing Republicans trailing in key races.

Trump told reporters, 'We have to get the Senate.' Tuesday will test whether a heavy personal campaign schedule can overcome a difficult polling environment for his party.

items.title: Early voting tops 54 million, already passing the entire 2022 midterm early total
items.summary:
More than 54 million Americans had voted before Election Day, according to the University of Florida Election Lab, about 8 million more than the 45.9 million early votes recorded in the 2022 midterms. The total includes in-person early ballots and mail ballots already returned.

In states that report party registration, Democrats accounted for roughly 43-44% of early votes and Republicans about 31-32%, with the rest independent or other. Texas alone passed 7.7 million early ballots, and Ohio set its own midterm record with more than 1.7 million early votes.

Election Lab director Michael McDonald said the early electorate looks younger, more diverse and more independent than in past midterms.

Experts caution that early totals show who voted, not how they voted. They are a sign of high interest in a midterm, not a forecast of who controls Congress.

items.title: Sen. Chris Murphy is awake and alert after a stroke, with no new medical update Monday
items.summary:
Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut remained hospitalized Monday after a stroke on Saturday, with no new clinical update beyond his office's statement on Sunday. His chief of staff said he is awake and alert at Johns Hopkins, responding well to treatment, and that doctors are optimistic he will make a full recovery.

Murphy, 53, first felt numbness in his arm on Saturday afternoon while at his son's hockey game and was taken to a local hospital, where the stroke was discovered. He was then transferred to Baltimore for monitoring. The type of stroke and any discharge timeline have not been disclosed.

Murphy is not on the ballot Tuesday, but he had been campaigning for other Democrats, including a planned New Hampshire stop on Sunday that was overtaken by the hospitalization.

Colleagues from both parties sent well wishes over the weekend. Any further word on his condition will come from his office, and Monday's coverage repeated Sunday's statement rather than adding new medical detail.

items.title: Dow rises alone as tech stocks slide for a third straight day
items.summary:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.41% to close at 51,983.98 on Monday, even as the broader tech selloff deepened. The S&P 500 fell 0.51% to 7,541.40 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 1.07% to 25,164.32, its third straight steep decline.

Chip stocks led the drop, with the S&P technology index down 2.7% and a semiconductor fund down nearly 4%. Intel fell about another 9% after a plunge on Friday, Marvell fell about 13%, and AMD fell 7%. Defensive and travel names rose instead, including Walmart, McDonald's, Sherwin-Williams and the major airlines, helped by cheaper oil.

Gold rose 1.5% to about $3,955 an ounce after falling to its lowest level in more than a year on Friday, and the 10-year Treasury yield stood at 4.92%.

The split picture — old-economy stocks up, AI-linked stocks down — has defined the market since October's selloff, and this week's election and earnings will test whether buyers return to tech.

items.title: Oil plunges more than 7% as hopes grow for U.S.-Iran talks
items.summary:
Oil posted its biggest drop in three months on Monday. West Texas Intermediate fell 7.4% to settle at $96.46 a barrel, back below $100, and Brent fell 7.6% to $104.77.

The move followed reports that Iran's leadership approved pursuing negotiations and that President Trump told Israel's prime minister he wanted to let talks play out. Iran's foreign minister said a proposal being worked on in Qatar could reopen the Strait of Hormuz in as little as two days if Washington meets conditions including ending the naval blockade and lifting oil sanctions.

European gas futures fell sharply as well, and U.S. heating oil had its steepest drop in six months. OPEC+ met virtually on Sunday and left December production unchanged.

Brent had briefly reached $118 in October, with a large share of that price reflecting war risk. If talks stall, traders warn that premium could return just as quickly.

items.title: Palantir revenue nearly doubles, and U.S. business sales pass government sales for the first time
items.summary:
Palantir reported third-quarter results after the close on Monday that beat expectations by a wide margin. Revenue rose 96% from a year earlier to $2.313 billion, above the roughly $2.18 billion analysts expected, and profit rose to $1.13 billion, or 44 cents a share.

The milestone in the report was the mix. U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, passing U.S. government revenue of $953 million for the first time in the company's history. Total U.S. revenue rose 119% to $1.937 billion, and quarterly revenue passed $2 billion for the first time.

Palantir raised its full-year revenue outlook to about $8.53 billion and guided fourth-quarter revenue above expectations. Shares rose modestly in after-hours trading.

One caution flagged by analysts is new contract growth: total contract value rose only about 6%, so investors will watch whether today's revenue surge turns into a durable order book.

items.title: Apple beats earnings in its new CEO's first quarter, but the stock still slips
items.summary:
Apple reported fiscal fourth-quarter results after the close on Monday that topped Wall Street forecasts. Revenue rose 12% to $114.5 billion, a September-quarter record, and earnings rose 14% to $2.10 a share, helped by a small benefit from tariff refunds.

iPhone revenue rose 17% to $57.58 billion, also a September-quarter record, Mac revenue rose 24%, and services hit an all-time high at $31.57 billion. Sales in Greater China rose 21% but came in below expectations, and iPad and wearables revenue fell. This was the first quarter under new CEO John Ternus.

Despite the beat, Apple shares closed the regular session down 1.83% at $338.32, caught in the day's broader tech selloff, and were little changed in early after-hours trading.

The December quarter is Apple's biggest of the year. Analysts will focus on holiday iPhone demand and whether China sales recover to forecast.

items.title: Oracle files to raise $20 billion in stock and bonds to pay for its AI build-out
items.summary:
Oracle filed Monday to raise $20 billion — $10 billion in new common stock and $10 billion in senior notes — to help fund its costly AI and cloud infrastructure expansion. The money is for general purposes including capital spending, debt repayment and acquisitions, according to the filings.

Investors did not welcome the dilution. Shares fell about 6% during the day, extending a decline of roughly a third so far in 2026. The bond sale will be split into six parts maturing between 2029 and 2046, with pricing not yet set.

The raise uses the full $20 billion of extra funding capacity Oracle outlined at its investor day on October 28 for its fiscal 2027-2030 AI cycle. The company carried about $125 billion in borrowings as of August 31 and is targeting revenue above $225 billion by fiscal 2030.

Oracle says free cash flow should turn positive in the second half of fiscal 2028. Until then, it is asking shareholders and bond buyers to fund the build-out up front.

items.title: Bitcoin holds up after the record $6.3 billion Binance hack as withdrawals reopen
items.summary:
Bitcoin traded around $78,300 on Monday, holding up better than many expected after Binance disclosed a $6.3 billion hack last week — the largest exchange theft on record. Binance says users lost no money, and it has replaced about 90-95% of the stolen assets from its own funds.

Withdrawals, which were paused after the breach, began reopening in phases on Sunday, starting with Bitcoin and 14 other networks. About $3 billion of the stolen assets have been frozen by partner exchanges, including $2.3 billion in stablecoins.

The FBI and blockchain firms have linked the attack to TraderTraitor, a group tied to North Korea that was also linked to last year's Bybit breach. Analysts tracking the stolen funds say most of the Bitcoin has not moved, though some stolen Solana began converting into Bitcoin over the weekend.

Traders are still paying more for downside protection, a sign the market is relieved but not relaxed. Binance's fuller proof-of-reserves update is the next credibility test.

items.title: Investigators say the Florida Learjet may have broken apart before it hit the ground
items.summary:
Federal investigators said Monday that the Learjet that crashed in Palm Beach County on Sunday, killing all nine people aboard, may have begun breaking up before impact. Debris is spread over about half a mile, and rain has been filling the impact crater with water, slowing recovery.

The charter flight left Austin, Texas, on Sunday morning bound for the Bahamas. The crew reported light clear ice and moderate turbulence at 35,000 feet, then asked to climb because of more precipitation. About 20 seconds later came a mayday, and tracking data showed an extremely fast descent.

Families on Monday identified the passengers as Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, their children Emma, 2, and Charlie, 4, the children's nanny Anita Maria Cetina, and a couple, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr. The co-pilot was Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, 20, of Boca Raton. About 400 to 600 people were displaced from a nearby mobile home park, and roughly 100 homes were evacuated.

No cause has been given. Weather and icing are a major focus, and officials have cautioned against early conclusions about the crew.

items.title: South Florida flooding called a 1,000-year event after 20 inches of rain in a day
items.summary:
Parts of Brevard County received about 20 inches of rain in 24 hours, an amount forecasters described as a one-in-a-thousand-year event for that area. All of South Florida stayed under a flood watch through Monday evening, with more rain possible.

Brevard County closed schools for the day, Florida Tech cancelled classes into Tuesday, and Melbourne issued a precautionary boil-water notice after a water main break. Palm Bay also lost water service in places after a separate main break, and rescue crews handled repeated calls for drivers stranded in high water.

Forecasters blamed a mix of autumn high tides, a recent full moon, and low pressure near the Bahamas interacting with high pressure to the north. Gusts reached near 50 mph and waves topped sea walls in places.

Rain chances stay elevated on Election Day in Palm Beach County, but forecasters do not expect a repeat of Monday's flooding rain. Officials also warned that standing floodwater raises the risk of bacterial infection.

items.title: Justice Department to send about 1,000 election monitors to polls in all 50 states
items.summary:
The Justice Department plans to send roughly 1,000 federal monitors to polling places in all 50 states on Tuesday, its largest election-monitoring effort ever and about three times the 388 sent in 2022. Monitors observe and take notes on possible violations of federal voting law and are not supposed to interfere with voters.

To reach that number, the department recruited staff from outside the Civil Rights Division, including criminal prosecutors — a break from past practice that has drawn criticism from voting-rights groups, who say it could intimidate voters and local officials. The NAACP sued to block the use of law enforcement agents as monitors, with a hearing held Monday afternoon.

Some local governments have already set limits, including counties in Minnesota that barred indoor observation and states that set distance rules from voting machines.

The full deployment list is not public and is expected on Election Day. Election officials have also warned that close races could bring disputes over counting and certification after the polls close.

items.title: Federal judge orders the Justice Department to stop pressuring election officials
items.summary:
A federal judge on Monday imposed a sweeping emergency order barring the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security from pressuring election officials in any state, including halting threats of criminal prosecution tied to voter-roll disputes.

The order follows letters sent by the department's Civil Rights Division to election officials in all states this summer, warning of legal action if officials knowingly allowed noncitizens to vote or to remain on the rolls. A separate ruling late Friday had already restrained the administration in the California ballot dispute.

The administration has argued its efforts are about election integrity and enforcing a 1996 law against noncitizen voting. State officials and voting-rights advocates say the pressure campaign, arriving days before the election, risks confusing voters and burdening the officials who must run it.

The rulings do not end the underlying lawsuits. They do mean that, for Tuesday's vote, states will run their elections under their own procedures while the legal fights continue afterward.

items.title: Voters head into the midterms in a sour mood on prices, even as jobs and growth look solid
items.summary:
On the eve of an election that decides control of Congress, voters are focused on the economy — and many are unhappy about it. High and rising prices are the top complaint, and many voters blame tariffs and the Iran war for keeping inflation stubborn.

The hard data tell a mixed story. Unemployment remains historically low, overall growth is solid, and business investment rose at a 12.7% annual pace last quarter on AI spending. But consumer prices and hourly pay have both risen about 5.5% since January 2025, and a University of Michigan sentiment gauge sits near a record low.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued last week that consumer behavior is stronger than the gloomy surveys suggest.

That gap between decent headline numbers and how households feel about grocery and energy bills is the political problem for the party in power, and it is the backdrop for every close race on Tuesday.

items.title: Severe storms target the Plains on Monday, with a tornado risk from Kansas to Oklahoma
items.summary:
Five states — Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Missouri and Arkansas — were on alert Monday for severe storms, with an enhanced risk of tornadoes between Wichita and Oklahoma City. Forecasters expected supercells to form in south-central Kansas and western Oklahoma in the late afternoon as temperatures climbed into the 70s and low 80s.

The Storm Prediction Center put parts of Kansas, Oklahoma and north Texas at Level 2 of 5 for Monday afternoon and evening, with large hail, damaging winds and a few tornadoes possible along a cold front and dryline. Storm chasers following the setup warned some tornadoes could be strong if storms stay organized into the early evening.

Separate warnings covered wind gusts above 60 mph in parts of Texas, New Mexico, South Dakota and Wyoming, with possible tree damage and power outages.

The threat shifts into the Deep South on Election Day, bringing heavy rain to Louisiana, Mississippi, Arkansas and Alabama, before spreading into the Midwest on Wednesday.

items.title: Ohio smashes its midterm early-voting record before Election Day
items.summary:
More than 1.7 million Ohioans had already voted by the close of early voting, a new record for a midterm in the state, beating the 1.5 million mark set in 2022. Nearly 1.1 million voted in person and about 632,000 returned mail ballots.

More than 104,000 absentee ballots are still outstanding. They must be received by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day to count — Ohio no longer has a grace period for ballots arriving late, so at this point they should be hand-delivered, not mailed.

Election officials credited heightened interest and record advertising, with high-profile races for governor between Vivek Ramaswamy and Amy Acton and for U.S. Senate between Jon Husted and Sherrod Brown driving turnout.

Unaffiliated voters made up the largest share of the early vote. Final turnout will depend on how many of the record early voters are joined by Election Day voters on Tuesday.

items.title: Election Day is Tuesday: what Cuyahoga County voters need to know
items.summary:
Polls in Ohio are open Tuesday, November 3, from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., and anyone in line at 7:30 p.m. can still vote. There was no early voting on Monday — in-person early voting ended Sunday afternoon.

On Election Day you must vote at your assigned polling place, and the Cuyahoga County Board of Elections warns that a number of polling locations changed for this election, including in the Solon area. Check your precinct and sample ballot with the Board's lookup tool before you go, and bring acceptable photo ID — an Ohio license showing a former address is still valid if your current address is on the poll list.

If you still hold a mail ballot, do not mail it now. Hand-deliver it to the Board of Elections at 1803 Superior Ave. in Cleveland by 7:30 p.m. Tuesday.

Voters will choose a governor, a U.S. senator, other state and local officials, and local issues. The Board can be reached at 216-443-VOTE.

items.title: Short-handed Thunder visit the Cavs tonight at Rocket Arena
items.summary:
The Cavaliers host the Oklahoma City Thunder tonight at 7 p.m. at Rocket Arena, on Peacock and NBCSN. Cleveland is 4-2 and unbeaten at home at 3-0, coming off a 136-111 win at Milwaukee on Saturday. The game had not been played as of Monday evening — this is a preview, not a result.

Both teams are short-handed. For Cleveland, Peyton Watson is questionable with hamstring tightness, while Jaylon Tyson is out with an ankle sprain and Nae'Qwan Tomlin is out with a back injury. Oklahoma City, also 4-2, lists six players out, including Chet Holmgren, Jalen Williams, Alex Caruso and Cason Wallace.

The Thunder have lost two straight and scored under 100 points in both, while Shai Gilgeous-Alexander is averaging 26 points a game. Cleveland was favored by about 3.5 to 4.5 points.

The same two teams meet again Wednesday in Oklahoma City, making tonight the first half of an unusual home-and-home in back-to-back stops.

items.title: Browns humbled in Pittsburgh as the Steelers take the AFC North lead
items.summary:
Cleveland's 27-6 loss at Pittsburgh on Sunday was its most lopsided defeat of the season. The Browns fell to 5-3, while the Steelers improved to 6-2 and took sole possession of first place in the AFC North.

Pittsburgh ran for 200 yards, led by Jaylen Warren's 143 yards and a touchdown, and built a 20-6 halftime lead. Cleveland's first three possessions ended in two lost fumbles and a three-and-out, the offense managed only 34 rushing yards, and Deshaun Watson was sacked eight times. Harold Fannin Jr. was a bright spot with 10 catches for 154 yards, though he also lost a fumble.

Head coach Todd Monken said the team earned the result and is capable of much better. All five of Cleveland's wins this season have come by four points or fewer.

The Browns travel to New Orleans to face the Saints on Sunday, November 8, at 1 p.m. A win there would keep them firmly in the wild-card picture heading into the second half of the season.

items.title: Buckeyes must bounce back Saturday against a dangerous Oregon team
items.summary:
Ohio State's margin for error is gone. The Buckeyes, 6-2 and 4-1 in the Big Ten after a 30-18 loss at USC, host Oregon on Saturday at 3:30 p.m. at Ohio Stadium on CBS, and likely need to win all four remaining November games to keep their conference title and playoff hopes alive.

Ohio State opened as a favorite of roughly 7.5 to 9.5 points, depending on the sportsbook. Oregon is 5-3 after beating Northwestern, and is now led by quarterback Dylan Raiola — a former Ohio State commit — after starter Dante Moore was lost for the season with a severe concussion in September. Raiola threw for 336 yards and three touchdowns against Northwestern.

The USC loss still stings in Columbus: Ohio State outgained the Trojans and held the ball for nearly 40 minutes, yet scored only one touchdown on 18 red-zone plays.

Freshman quarterback Luke Fahey, who made his first start at USC, and receiver Jeremiah Smith, who set the Big Ten record with his 40th career touchdown catch in that game, will be central to the response.

items.title: Cleveland misses out on $7.8 million in federal money to make homes lead-safe
items.summary:
The federal government has denied Cleveland's application for a $7.8 million lead-hazard grant, after a risk review of how the city manages federal housing money — including reporting, meeting goals and finishing work on time. City Council member Kris Harsh called the denial terrible news.

The timing is difficult. Three older federal lead grants are winding down with no replacement lined up: a $9.7 million Glenville grant closing at the end of November, a $2 million healthy-homes grant closing next June, and a $5.7 million citywide grant closing next July. Federal officials have also raised concerns about the city's community development block grant funds.

The denial does not change landlords' obligations. Rental homes built before 1978 must still be certified as lead-safe, and the city says it will keep enforcing that ordinance.

Cleveland also lost a $3.3 million state lead grant in February for slow spending. For a city with one of the nation's most serious lead-paint problems in older housing, the gap between the rules on paper and the money to fix homes is widening.

baby.tip: Day two with a newborn: start a simple log on your phone — feed times, wet diapers and dirty diapers. It feels like overkill at 3 a.m., but the pediatrician's first questions at Benji's first visit (usually a few days after discharge) are exactly those counts, and nobody remembers them on no sleep. One shared note that both Mike and Kelly can add to beats two tired memories.
baby.fact: A newborn sees best at about 8 to 12 inches — almost exactly the distance between a feeding baby's face and a parent's face. Benji's vision is still blurry and he prefers high-contrast patterns and faces, which is why face-to-face time at feeding distance is, quite literally, his favorite view in the world right now.
baby.fun: Name tidbit for the day: Benjamin is a Hebrew name meaning 'son of the right hand,' and in the Bible Benjamin was the youngest of twelve brothers — a fitting name for the newest and youngest Smiley. Today's tiny mission: tell Benji the story of his name once, out loud, even if he sleeps through the whole thing.
